passage: Nursery note, Tuesday. During snack time, Ramesh lined up his grapes and touched each one: "One, two, three, four, five." Jatin had three. Ramesh looked from plate to plate and said, "I got more! Jatin has less." Jatin frowned and counted his own twice, getting three both times. I asked what would make them the same. Ramesh thought for a while, then slid two grapes across. They counted together, and both plates had five. Next week I will add a bead basket to the snack corner. 🙂

qa.q: How many grapes did Jatin have at first?
qa.a: Jatin had three grapes.

qa.q: What was Jatin probably feeling when he frowned and counted his grapes twice?
qa.a: He was likely puzzled and a bit upset at being told he had less, so he counted twice to test Ramesh's claim.

qa.q: What small step could the teacher try next to keep this counting going?
qa.a: She could give pairs of children beads or blocks to share out and ask, "Who has more? How can we make it the same?"

qa.q: What would change if Ramesh had only glanced at the plates instead of counting one by one?
qa.a: He might have guessed wrongly, and the idea of making the plates equal would not have come from real numbers.

grounding: It shows a child counting objects one by one and comparing which plate has more or less.

passage: At the Sunday haat in their kasba, Nani bought a paper cone of peanuts and tipped some into each child's palm. Sonali, five, counted aloud, pressing each nut with her thumb: "Ek, do, teen, char, paanch, chhe." Her little brother Kishore had a heap too, but kept losing his place after three. "Mine is more," he declared, because his pile looked wider. Sonali laid both piles in two rows on Nani's cloth bag. Her row stretched past his by two nuts. Kishore stared. "Yours is longer," he admitted, and held out his hand. Nani chuckled and gave him two more.

qa.q: Where did Nani buy the peanuts?
qa.a: At the Sunday haat in their kasba.

qa.q: Why did Kishore think his pile was more?
qa.a: He felt confident his pile was more because it looked wider, judging by looks rather than counting, since he kept losing his place after three.

qa.q: How could Nani help Kishore count past three?
qa.a: She could count slowly with him, touching each nut the way Sonali did, or line the nuts in a row so he can keep his place.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Kishore's claim?
qa.a: She seems to find it worth checking rather than arguing about, so she lays the nuts in rows to show the difference plainly.

grounding: It shows a five-year-old counting and using rows to show which pile has more.

passage: On a grey Saturday in Rotterdam, Elif and her neighbour Nour sat on the back step sharing a bag of cherries. Elif made two piles. "Four for you, four for me," she said, counting each red stem. Nour pointed. "Yours has a big one." "Big is not more," Elif said slowly, frowning. "More is the counting." She counted both piles again, her finger bouncing. Four and four. Nour shrugged and swapped one big cherry for a small one anyway, and they both grinned.

qa.q: How many cherries were in each pile?
qa.a: There were four cherries in each pile.

qa.q: What does Elif's slow frown suggest when Nour mentions the big cherry?
qa.a: She seems to be working out the difference between size and number and wants to be sure before she answers.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby build on Elif's idea?
qa.a: They could ask, "Which pile has more cherries, and which pile is heavier?" so she can explore size and number as two different things.

qa.q: How does Nour see fairness differently from Elif?
qa.a: Nour judges by the size of the cherries while Elif judges by the count, so the swap lets both of them feel it is even. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child using counting to decide which amount is more, separate from size.

passage: At the anganwadi, Deepak Sir poured jaggery chana onto two leaves. 'Irfan, which leaf has more?' Irfan pointed at the bigger heap. 'This one!' 'Let's check.' Irfan counted slowly, touching each chana. 'One, two... seven.' Then the other: 'One... four.' He frowned, then brightened. 'Seven is more! Four is less.' Deepak Sir moved two chana across. Irfan counted again and shouted, 'Now it's five and six!'

qa.q: How many chana did Irfan count on the first leaf?
qa.a: He counted seven chana on the first leaf.

qa.q: Why did Irfan brighten after frowning?
qa.a: He felt pleased when counting confirmed his guess and he understood that seven is more than four.

qa.q: What could Deepak Sir try next to stretch Irfan's counting?
qa.a: He could make two heaps that look similar in size, so Irfan must count rather than just look to find which is more.

qa.q: How might the other children at the anganwadi react to Irfan's shout?
qa.a: They might get curious and want a turn counting and comparing heaps themselves.

grounding: Illustrates a young child counting objects and comparing quantities as more and less, in an anganwadi.

passage: My brother Gautam is five and counts everything now. Yesterday he counted the stairs to our flat: 'Twenty-two!' At tea, Amma gave us grapes. Gautam lined his up and then mine. 'Kunal Bhaiya has more,' he said, pointing at my longer row. I only had one more, but he counted anyway, twice. Amma gave him one extra. He counted again, nodded, and ate them one by one.

qa.q: How many stairs did Gautam count?
qa.a: He counted twenty-two stairs.

qa.q: What does Gautam counting twice suggest he was feeling about the grapes?
qa.a: He seemed anxious that he might be getting less than his brother, so he counted twice to be sure before complaining.

qa.q: How could Amma use grape time to help Gautam learn more about numbers?
qa.a: She could ask him how many more he needs to be equal, turning snack time into a small counting game.

qa.q: How does Kunal see his little brother's counting?
qa.a: Kunal seems a little amused but interested, noticing how carefully Gautam now counts and compares.

grounding: Shows a young child counting and comparing quantities, described by his older brother.

passage: Monday: Yamini, four, counted the steps up to her Ajji Urmila's flat: "One, two, three, seven, ten!" and ran up two at a time. Thursday: Ajji put laddoos on two plates. Yamini touched each one as she counted: "One, two, three, four." She did the other plate: "One, two." The next Sunday: Ajji put out the plates again. Yamini didn't count at all. She pointed. "That one has more. I want that one." Ajji laughed and gave her the smaller plate first.

qa.q: What did Yamini touch as she counted on Thursday?
qa.a: Each laddoo on the plates.

qa.q: What might Yamini have wanted when she pointed at the bigger plate?
qa.a: She wanted the plate with more laddoos and seemed confident she could tell without counting.

qa.q: How could Ajji Urmila keep building Yamini's counting?
qa.a: Keep giving small everyday chances to count and compare, like steps, laddoos or shoes, and let her check by touching.

qa.q: How might Ajji Urmila see Yamini's progress over the week?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and amused, seeing her move from jumbled numbers to spotting "more" at a glance.

grounding: Shows a young child moving from jumbled counting to one-by-one counting to comparing which plate has more.

passage: Black clouds rolled over the village, and Ramesh had to get the hens into the coop before the storm. "Count them in, Mohit!" His son, five, stood at the little door. "One, two, three…" The first drops fell. Hens ran in, flapping. "…seven, eight." Mohit frowned. "Papa, we have nine. One is less!" Ramesh looked round and found the brown hen under the cart. Mohit counted again. "Nine! All here."

qa.q: How many hens should there have been?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he said "One is less!"?
qa.a: He was worried that a hen was missing and wanted his father to find it before the rain.

qa.q: How could Ramesh make the most of Mohit's counting?
qa.a: Give him the counting job every evening and thank him when his count catches a missing hen.

qa.q: What would change if Mohit hadn't counted?
qa.a: The brown hen might have been left out in the storm without anyone noticing.

grounding: Shows a young child counting hens under time pressure and noticing when there is one less.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Kunal, five, and his little brother Siddharth each got a bowl of grapes. Kunal peered into both. "His has more!" "They're the same," said their mother. Kunal tipped his own onto the table and counted: "One, two… eleven." Then he counted Siddharth's. "Eleven." He looked puzzled. "But his bowl looks full." "His bowl is smaller," said their mother. Kunal put his grapes back and said, "Same. Okay."

qa.q: How many grapes did Kunal count in his own bowl?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did Kunal look puzzled after counting?
qa.a: He expected Siddharth to have more, so finding the same number confused him.

qa.q: How could their mother help Kunal next time he thinks something is unfair?
qa.a: Encourage him to count again, as he did, so he can check "more" and "less" for himself.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth when Kunal says his has more?
qa.a: He might feel worried his grapes could be taken, and relieved when the count shows they are the same.

grounding: Shows a young child using counting to check whether a bowl really holds more.

passage:
"Pema, give me five lemons," Sarika Aunty said at her vegetable stall.
Pema, five, counted, touching each one. "One, two, three, four, five."
"Good. Now, who has more, you or me?" Aunty held up three.
Pema looked. "Me! Five is more."
"How many more?"
Pema pointed at her lemons, then at Aunty's. She pushed her extra two to the side. "Two more!"
"Clever girl. Now give one to me."
"Now I have four, you have four! Same!"
"Same. So who gets the free guava?"
Pema grinned. "Both!"

qa.q: How many lemons did Sarika Aunty ask for?
qa.a: Five lemons.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when she said 'Same!'?
qa.a: Pema felt excited and proud, noticing the numbers had become equal.

qa.q: How did Sarika Aunty turn the sale into a counting lesson?
qa.a: She asked who had more and how many more, and let Pema move lemons to see equal amounts.

qa.q: How might Sarika Aunty feel when Pema says 'Both!'?
qa.a: Sarika Aunty probably felt amused and happy at Pema's clever answer.

grounding: At a vegetable stall, a five-year-old counts and compares quantities with a shopkeeper.

passage: Kindergarten note, Pongal week. We gave each child sugarcane pieces at snack time. Karthik (5) had four; his friend Ravi had six. Karthik counted both piles twice, frowned, and said, "Ravi has more. Two more." Last month he would have said "same", because his pieces looked long. I asked what would make it fair. He moved one of Ravi's pieces to his own pile. "Now five and five." Ravi agreed. I'll send home a counting game for the holidays. — Abhinav Sir

qa.q: How many pieces did Karthik have?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he frowned at the piles?
qa.a: Karthik felt it was unfair and a little annoyed that Ravi had more.

qa.q: How did Abhinav Sir build on Karthik's counting?
qa.a: He asked what would make it fair, letting Karthik move pieces to make equal piles.

qa.q: How might Ravi feel about giving up a piece?
qa.a: Ravi agreed, so he probably felt fine, perhaps happy that it was fair.

grounding: A Pongal-week kindergarten note records a five-year-old counting to compare more and less.

passage: At Baisakhi harvest in their village near Ludhiana, Jasleen tied wheat into bundles while her son Lokesh, five, sat on the cart. "Count them for me," she called. Lokesh pointed. "One, two, three… eleven!" He had skipped seven. Jasleen laughed. "Again, slowly. Touch each one." This time he touched every bundle and got twelve. "Mamma, that side has more than this side!" "How do you know?" "Because this side is only five." Jasleen tossed him a sugarcane stick. "My accountant."

qa.q: How many bundles did Lokesh count the second time?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Jasleen called him 'My accountant'?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt proud and pleased at the praise.

qa.q: What tip helped Lokesh count correctly?
qa.a: Counting slowly and touching each bundle, so he didn't skip any.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel as Lokesh compares the two sides?
qa.a: Jasleen probably feels amused and proud, seeing him understand more and less.

grounding: At a village harvest, a five-year-old learns to count carefully and compare quantities.

passage:
On New Year's morning in Osaka, Kwame set out a plate of mochi for Hana and her cousin.

"You have five, and Kenji has three," Kwame said. "Who has more?"

Hana touched each one. "One, two, three, four, five." Then Kenji's. "One, two, three." She grinned. "Me! I have more."

Kenji's lip trembled. Hana looked at the plates, then moved one mochi across. "Now I have four and you have four. Same."

qa.q: How many mochi did Kenji have at first?
qa.a: Kenji had three.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when she saw Kenji's lip tremble?
qa.a: Hana felt sorry for Kenji and wanted things to be fair, so she moved one mochi across.

qa.q: How can Kwame build on Hana's counting?
qa.a: He could ask her more "more or less" questions at meals and let her count and share items herself.

qa.q: How might Kenji feel when Hana made the plates the same?
qa.a: Kenji would likely feel happy and relieved to have the same as Hana.

grounding: On New Year's morning, a child counts mochi, compares more and less, and evens out the plates.

passage:
It was sports week at the kindergarten, and the hall was full of coloured beanbags. Dhruv Sir put two baskets on the floor.

"Nandini, which basket has more?"

Nandini looked. The red basket looked fuller. But she tipped both out and counted. Red: six. Blue: eight.

"Blue has more!" she said. "The red one looked bigger, but it only has six."

Dhruv Sir gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: How many beanbags were in the blue basket?
qa.a: Blue had eight.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when she found blue had more?
qa.a: Nandini felt surprised and proud, having checked by counting instead of guessing.

qa.q: How can Dhruv Sir keep supporting Nandini's counting?
qa.a: He could give her more sets to compare and praise her for counting to check.

qa.q: How might Dhruv Sir feel about Nandini's answer?
qa.a: Dhruv Sir was likely impressed and pleased, giving her a thumbs up.

grounding: During sports week, a child counts beanbags to find out which basket really has more.

passage:
I'm Uday, Manoj's cousin. On Diwali, Manoj, who's five, was given a box of laddoos to share with all of us cousins.

He counted us: "One, two, three, four, five, six." Then he counted the laddoos: five.

He frowned. "One less." He looked at the box for a long time. Then he broke his own laddoo in half and gave me half.

I'm not sure if he was sad about it. He didn't say.

qa.q: How many laddoos were in the box?
qa.a: There were five laddoos.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when he found one less laddoo?
qa.a: Uday wasn't sure, but Manoj seemed worried and thoughtful, looking at the box for a long time.

qa.q: How could an adult support Manoj's counting and sharing?
qa.a: Praise him for counting and noticing, and help him find fair ways to share when numbers don't match.

qa.q: How does Uday see Manoj's choice?
qa.a: Uday noticed the kind choice but couldn't tell how Manoj felt about giving up half his laddoo.

grounding: A cousin watches a child count sweets and people during Diwali, notice one less, and solve it by sharing.

passage:
First Sunday of the summer holidays: Eshaan counted the mangoes in the basket, "One, two, five, three!" and pointed at the same mango twice. Ritu laughed.
Wednesday: Nani lined the mangoes up in a row. Eshaan touched each one as he counted. "Seven!"
The next Sunday: Nani gave Eshaan three mangoes and Ritu five. Eshaan looked at both piles and frowned. "Ritu has more. Not fair." Nani moved one across. "Now?" He counted again. "Four and four. Same!"

qa.q: How many mangoes did Nani first give Eshaan on the last Sunday?
qa.a: She gave Eshaan three mangoes.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when he saw Ritu's bigger pile?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and was a little annoyed, because he could now tell that Ritu had more.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan count correctly by Wednesday?
qa.a: Lining the mangoes up in a row let him touch each one once, so he didn't count any twice.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu when Eshaan miscounts at first?
qa.a: Ritu finds it funny, perhaps feeling grown-up because counting is already easy for Ritu.

grounding: Shows a young child moving from muddled counting to comparing which pile has more during mango season.
